{
  "summary": "This PR replaces string-based argument registration and lookup in ArgsManager with strongly typed setting declarations via a new common::Setting class. Settings define their name, type, and default value in dedicated header files, replacing AddArg and Get*Arg calls with Setting::Register and Setting::Get across the codebase.",
  "problem": "Setting names and types are specified as loose string keys and varied function calls across registration and retrieval points. Typos in argument names are not caught at compile time, retrieval types can become inconsistent across call sites, and default values can drift between help text strings and retrieval fallbacks.",
  "evidence": [
    "PR description: 'currently settings are registered and retrieved like argsman.AddArg(\"-pid=...\") and args.GetPathArg(\"-pid\")... nothing checks that setting names are spelled correctly, or that default values are used consistently in the help string and retrieval sites, or that settings are retrieved with consistent types.'",
    "Linked to ArgsManager type and range checking design discussion in #22978."
  ],

The vast bulk of the change is an automated, scripted-diff commit converting existing AddArg and GetArg calls and generating modular *_settings.h headers.",
  "changed_since_previous": "",
  "card": "This PR introduces a compile-time typed Setting template mechanism to replace raw string lookups in ArgsManager across the codebase. Currently, configuration settings are looked up with string keys like GetArg(\"-foo\"), which leaves typos uncaught by the compiler, risks inconsistent retrieval types, and allows default values to diverge from help text. The change defines settings declaratively and migrates callsites to typed Setting::Register and Setting::Get invocations via a large scripted diff. It also lays the groundwork for structured options structs and runtime validation discussed in issue #22978.",

result.summary: This PR replaces string-based argument registration and lookup in ArgsManager with strongly typed setting declarations via a new common::Setting class. Settings define their name, type, and default value in dedicated header files, replacing AddArg and Get*Arg calls with Setting::Register and Setting::Get across the codebase.
result.problem: Setting names and types are specified as loose string keys and varied function calls across registration and retrieval points. Typos in argument names are not caught at compile time, retrieval types can become inconsistent across call sites, and default values can drift between help text strings and retrieval fallbacks.
evidence: PR description: 'currently settings are registered and retrieved like argsman.AddArg("-pid=...") and args.GetPathArg("-pid")... nothing checks that setting names are spelled correctly, or that default values are used consistently in the help string and retrieval sites, or that settings are retrieved with consistent types.'
Linked to ArgsManager type and range checking design discussion in #22978.
result.scope_notes: The PR touches 100 files and adds over 3,700 lines, but the core logic is in the Setting class (src/common/setting.h and setting_internal.h). The vast bulk of the change is an automated, scripted-diff commit converting existing AddArg and GetArg calls and generating modular *_settings.h headers.
result.card: This PR introduces a compile-time typed Setting template mechanism to replace raw string lookups in ArgsManager across the codebase. Currently, configuration settings are looked up with string keys like GetArg("-foo"), which leaves typos uncaught by the compiler, risks inconsistent retrieval types, and allows default values to diverge from help text. The change defines settings declaratively and migrates callsites to typed Setting::Register and Setting::Get invocations via a large scripted diff. It also lays the groundwork for structured options structs and runtime validation discussed in issue #22978.
